# How Vasubandhu got its accent back

The ASCII form *vasubandhu* is missing something. **Vasubandhu** restores ​the marks the source language used to distinguish this name from a thousand others — and those marks change how the name is read, pronounced, and understood. This post explains, with the ‌full scholarly record behind it, what each restored mark preserves: the Devanagari evidence, the reconstructed sound, the myths the name carries, and the mechanical logic of what each restored mark preserves. By ‌the end, the marks in Vasubandhu will look less like ornaments and more like what they are — recovered evidence, pinned back in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Vasubandhu
- ​**ASCII form:** vasubandhu
- **Meaning:** "The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school"
- **Domain of influence:** Abhidharma, Yogacara
- **Pantheon:** Buddhist
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** वसुबन्धु (Devanagari)

The name means "The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school".

**Vasubandhu** is abhidharma, yogacara. The name means "The celebrated Buddhist ​scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school" and belongs to the buddhist tradition.

## Mythology

The stories ​of Vasubandhu place abhidharma, yogacara at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Vasubandhu appears in buddhist tradition as abhidharma, yogacara. The name's meaning, "The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author ​of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Vasubandhu in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the ​name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Vasubandhu survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. ‌The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Vasubandhu gives the figure a stable name around which these variants ​orbit.

### Three Years in Seclusion (The Kośa)

The Tibetan biographies recount that Vasubandhu withdrew into seclusion to master the Abhidharma of the Kashmir Sarvāstivādins, and emerged with the Abhidharmakośa — six ‌hundred verses (kārikā) of flawless eight-syllable metre that summarized the entire system. When the Kashmir masters admired the verses but missed their own subtlety, he added an auto-commentary (bhāṣya) of his own ​in which, tradition says, he quietly refuted them. The Kośa became what it remains: the one Abhidharma text every later school — Theravāda, Mahāyāna, and the Tibetan lineages — had to study, ‌debate, or answer, translated in its entirety into Chinese by Xuanzang and memorized in fragments by generations of monks from Kashmir to Kyoto. Its author's own allegiance was already drifting as he ​wrote: the commentary, tradition says, shows the Sautrāntika reservations that would later make his conversion credible. To condense a library into verse, and the verse into a single lifetime, is the legend's ‌whole point: scholarship can be a kind of asceticism.

### The Begging Letter of Asaṅga (Conversion)

Vasubandhu had mocked the Mahāyāna as a corruption of the Buddha's teaching, calling its scriptures fabrications. His ​elder half-brother Asaṅga, already a great Yogācāra teacher, sent him no rebuttal — only a note reporting that he was dying, and begging Vasubandhu to recite the Mahāyāna sūtras for him. ‌Struck by the affection of the request, Vasubandhu read them, found them profound, and entered the Mahāyāna himself. The story is hagiography — no Indian source records it independently — yet it ​encodes the tradition's own account of its greatest conversion: Vasubandhu did not abandon analysis for devotion. He turned the same razor-sharp mind to the 'mind-only' philosophy, composing the Twenty Verses (Viṁśikā) and ​the Thirty Verses (Triṁśikā) that define the Yogācāra, and the two halves of his career became one continuous argument about how carefully the world must be taken apart before it can be ‌seen whole.

### The Victory over Vasurāta (The Debate)

The biographies carry Vasubandhu to the courts of northern India, where the grammarian-philosopher Vasurāta, champion of an opposing school, had humiliated all comers. Vasubandhu ‌entered the contest — the tradition describes a great assembly of rival teachers and lay patrons gathered to watch — and his opponent was worsted. After the debate he was offered a ‌great patron's gold — and the legends insist that, as a monk, he spent the wealth on works of benefit to the saṅgha and on gifts to the poor. The story ​matters less as history than as the template it sets: the philosopher's victory is measured not in refutation but in what the victor refuses to keep. Every medieval debate culture of the ​Buddhist world — Nālandā's, Tibet's, Japan's — repeated this scene with Vasubandhu's name in it, and his reputation as the undefeated champion of two successive orthodoxies made the later conversion legend necessary: ‌only love, the tradition decided, could have beaten him.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Vasubandhu concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- ​**Name** — The restored form Vasubandhu, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Abhidharma, Yogacara

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Vasubandhu across media and ​centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Vasubandhu carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The Kośa stanza** ‌— A verse (kārikā) whose eight-syllable lines hold whole Abhidharma treatises — scholarship compressed into memorable sound
- **The begging bowl** — The monk's only equipment; Vasubandhu remained a bhikṣu all his ​life even while moving courts and schools
- **The letter from Asaṅga** — In the Tibetan biographies, the note that converted him — affection and mortality doing what doctrine could not
- **Treasury (kośa)** ​— The storehouse metaphor of the Abhidharmakośa: every dharma catalogued like treasure in a vault, each with its own nature

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex ‌corpus is yet assigned to Vasubandhu with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Buddhist name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary ​evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming वसुबन्धु, sanctuary or cult remains tied ‌to abhidharma and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

**Vasubandhu** ​is abhidharma, yogacara. The name means "The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school" and belongs to the buddhist tradition.

### The Conversion

Legend says his brother Asaṅga sent him a begging letter: ​compassion, not argument, turned the Kośa's author toward the Mahāyāna.

## A Meditation

To contemplate Vasubandhu is to hold the idea of abhidharma, Yogacara in the mind and to ask what ‌of it endures. The name means "The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school" — and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation ‌rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as abhidharma, Yogacara · The celebrated Buddhist scholar — author of the Abhidharmakośa, co-founder of the Yogācāra school.

Sit with the restored form ‌— Vasubandhu — and the diacritics themselves become the practice: each mark is a small act of attention, a refusal to let the plain ASCII form *vasubandhu* stand in for the ‌whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve in turn.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of ‌**Vasubandhu**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Devanagari rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *vasubandhu* and the ​restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic ‌and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently ‌in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **v**, **a**, **s**, **u**, **b**, **a**, **n**, **d**, **h**, **u** — so visitors can see exactly what is being ​carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

## Vasubandhu in Its Tradition

**Vasubandhu** does ​not stand alone. It belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is counted among 26 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Abhidharma, Yogacara — places it beside other figures who ​govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address ​bar shows **Vasubandhu**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored ‌name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Vasubandhu** is one such vote.
